newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels say they are marching on Kinshasa again.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels say they are marching on Kinshasa again.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's rebels said Sunday they were resuming their march on Zaire's capital, abandoning a pledge to South African President Nelson Mandela to halt their advance to give diplomacy a chance.

Kabila's "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha announced the move at a news conference ahead of a second face-to-face meeting between Mandela, Kabila and embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko on a South African ship Wednesday.

"Mobutu is a devil and a trickster and has used the talks to reinforce his troops, bring in UNITA (Angolan rebel) elements, former Rwandan troops and consolidate his position in Kinshasa," Karaha said in the rebel-held southern city of Lubumbashi.
"Our response to this is that we are abandoning our pledge and we are now advancing and will continue to advance. We shall now talk and fight, and fight and talk."
The rebels were last reported less than 200 km (125 miles) from the teeming capital of five million.
Diplomatic and political manoeuvring intensified ahead of Wednesday's meeting.

Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, tipped as a key player in any peace deal, promised personal initiatives to promote a quick, consensus transition -- after Mobutu supporters voted to give him back the job of speaker of Zaire's transitional parliament.

Karaha said the rebels might pull out of the South African peace initiative and storm Kinshasa if Monsengwo accepted the job of speaker -- the constitutional successor to the president in the event of death or incapacity.
The rebels, who took up arms in October and control three quarters of Africa's third largest country, insist that Mobutu step down and hand power to Kabila.
The radical opposition of Etienne Tshisekedi, the other main political force in parliament, walked out before Saturday's vote -- raising doubts as to whether it was binding.
Monsengwo, who is still popular in a country with a Roman Catholic majority, held the job of speaker at the height of Zaire's promised transition to democracy.

Some diplomats and politicians say he could step in and provide Mobutu with a dignified exit. Others say Monsengwo could act as a national mediator -- a role he played as speaker until ousted in July 1995.

"I will only accept if I have national and international guarantees," Monsengwo told a news conference in Belgium during a stopover on his way back to Kinshasa from the Vatican where he attended a conference. He did not elaborate.

The Vatican has yet to give its blessing to the move but Monsengwo promised initiatives to find a peaceful settlement. He gave no details but said these aimed "at a transition which has consensus support and is quick."

Mobutu supporters, fearing Monsengwo's popularity in the event of elections, joined forces with Tshisekedi supporters in 1995 to oust him. Tshisekedi supporters dismiss Monsengwo, archbishop of rebel-held Kisangani, as "Mobutist."
Mobutu, 66, has dominated the mineral-rich country at the heart of Africa for over three decades.
He returned to Kinshasa Saturday after talks in Gabon with fellow Central African leaders and Mandela's deputy president, Thabo Mbeki.

Mbeki said Mobutu and Kabila had agreed to attend fresh talks Wednesday. The first such meeting, on May 4, ended with Mobutu offering to hand power to an elected successor and Kabila demanding he stand down immediately.
